  1. Open your My GitHub account link. The card shows No personal GitHub account connected. ①
  2. Select Connect personal account. ②
  3. Your browser leaves Plane and opens GitHub’s authorization page. This full-page navigation is expected (the page cannot authorize inside Plane’s frame).
  4. On GitHub, check the account name shown, then approve the authorization.
  5. GitHub sends you back to the My GitHub account page.
Screenshot needed — gh-03-oauth-consent — GitHub's authorize screen during Connect personal account (needs a signed-in GitHub browser session). Capture later with npm run manual:capture -- --only gh-03-oauth-consent

Later visits show the card without the notice:

If it went wrong: see Connection errors below.

What happens behind the button

  • git-sync creates a single-use, expiring connection link bound to your Plane user (with PKCE, so the code GitHub returns is useless to anyone else).
  • After you approve, GitHub returns a code; git-sync exchanges it for a user token and asks GitHub who you are.
  • It stores your GitHub login and its stable numeric account ID. The ID is what counts: if you later rename your GitHub account, the link still points at the same account, and nobody who later takes your old username inherits your link.
  • The GitHub token is stored encrypted. git-sync refreshes it automatically when GitHub issues expiring tokens.
  • If an admin previously unlinked you, connecting again lifts that block.

Other ways a link can be created

  • An admin links you on the User links page (Part B, User links). The admin types your GitHub login; git-sync checks it with GitHub and stores the numeric ID. No token is stored in that case, so the link identifies you but cannot act as you on GitHub.
  • Automatic email match. When an event comes from a GitHub user who is not linked, and that user’s public GitHub email exactly matches the email of exactly one workspace member, git-sync links them and records Account matched by email in the audit log. Disconnecting yourself (below) prevents this from re-linking you automatically.

What your link changes — and what it does not

Being precise here saves a lot of “why does it say the bot did this?” questions.

Your link lets git-sync recognise you. Events from GitHub carry an authenticated sender (the GitHub account that caused the event). With your link, git-sync can map that sender to your Plane user. This is used for:

  • Smart Commit provenance: comments end with “via <sha> by <your login>”.
  • Translating GitHub @mentions and assignees on mirrored issues into Plane users (an unmapped login in a mention becomes a GitHub profile link; an unmapped assignee is simply dropped).
  • Deciding whether problem reports may contain details (some reports are only shown in full to linked members).
  • The repository picker an admin sees when mapping repositories (it lists repositories their account can access).
  • The {username} placeholder in a branch-name template, if your team uses one.

Changes that go from Plane to GitHub can be authored as you. When you change a mirrored Plane work item, and your stored GitHub token works for that repository, git-sync writes the GitHub side with your token. If the token is missing, expired beyond refresh or refused, it falls back to the App’s own identity (<app-slug>[bot]). Some steps, such as link-back comments, always come from the App.

Changes that go from GitHub to Plane appear as the git-sync service account in this release. The code can write to Plane as an individual user only when it holds that user’s Plane personal access token (PAT). No screen in this release stores one, so every Plane comment, state change, link and mirrored item created by git-sync shows the service (bot) user as its author. The audit log records this as Service account attribution with the reason no_stored_token. This is expected behavior, not a failure. The provenance line in Smart Commit comments tells readers who really did it.

Note: A Plane PAT and your GitHub link are two separate credentials. Linking GitHub does not create a Plane PAT, and the member account page has no field for one. Never paste a Plane PAT (or any token) into a commit, comment, chat or screenshot.

Example: Alex pushes WEB-42 #comment Checked at 320, 375 and 390 px widths. In Plane the comment appears under the git-sync service user and ends with “via 3b2335d by alex-dev”. Sam then edits the title of a mirrored Plane item; because Sam’s GitHub token works, the GitHub issue’s history shows sam-reviews made the edit.

Reconnect when the card says Needs re-authorization

GitHub can refuse a stored token: you revoked the authorization on GitHub, an organization policy changed, or the refresh token expired. git-sync then marks your link and the card shows:

The three states side by side:

Goal: restore a working authorization

Steps

  1. Open My GitHub account. The card shows Needs re-authorization. Reconnect your GitHub account to author changes as yourself. ①
  2. Select Reconnect. ②
  3. On GitHub, check the account and approve.
  4. Back on the card, confirm GitHub account: shows your login and the notice is gone.

Result: the same link is kept (same numeric ID) with a fresh token.

While the notice is shown, nothing breaks: git-sync keeps recognizing you as the event sender, and GitHub writes fall back to the App identity. The admin’s User links page shows the same flag next to your name.

Tip: Reconnecting with a different GitHub account replaces your link with that account, if it is not linked to someone else in the workspace.

Disconnect your personal account

Disconnecting is a personal action. It is different from the Disconnect button on an organization card in Workspace GitHub connection, which an admin uses to disconnect the whole installation and disables its mappings.

Goal: remove your personal link

Steps

  1. Open My GitHub account.
  2. Select Disconnect personal account.
  3. Read the confirmation: “Disconnect your GitHub account? Synced writes will use the service account until you reconnect.” ① Confirm. ②
  4. The card returns to No personal GitHub account connected.

Your browser shows this confirmation (text recorded from the running UI):

Note: “Disconnect your GitHub account? Synced writes will use the service account until you reconnect.” Choose OK to disconnect or Cancel to keep the link.

What disconnect does:

  • Asks GitHub to revoke the authorization (best effort; if GitHub cannot be reached, the local token is deleted anyway).
  • Deletes your stored GitHub token. Tokens are stored per Plane user, so this also ends personal GitHub authorship in your other workspaces until you connect again.
  • Removes your link in this workspace.
  • Records that you unlinked, so the automatic email match does not silently link you again.

What disconnect does not do: it does not delete branches, commits, PRs, comments, links on work items, or repository mappings. Your future events are simply treated as coming from an unmapped GitHub user. To stop the whole team’s integration, ask a workspace admin.

Connection errors

When the OAuth round trip fails, GitHub sends you back with an error, and the page shows one of these notices. The text is exact.

Notice on the page Cause What to do
This connection link has expired, was already used, or belongs to another Plane account. Start again. The single-use link timed out, was reused (for example the back button), or you returned signed in as a different Plane user Select Connect personal account again in the right Plane session
GitHub authorization was declined. You can connect again when ready. You pressed Cancel on GitHub Connect again when ready
Notice on the page Cause What to do
GitHub authorization could not be completed. Start again. The code exchange with GitHub failed Try once more; if it repeats, send the admin the time and this message
This GitHub account is already linked to another member in this workspace. Another Plane user in this workspace is linked to that GitHub account Check you used the right GitHub account; otherwise ask an admin to inspect User links
Ask the instance admin to configure the GitHub App client ID, client secret and App slug. OAuth is not configured for the App Ask the instance admin (God mode → GitHub App)
GitHub could not complete the connection. Check your account access and try again. GitHub refused the user lookup after authorization Retry; check your GitHub account is in good standing
The connection could not be completed. Try again; ask an instance admin to check the service if it keeps failing. Unexpected server error Retry once, then report
Personal account settings need workspace membership. You are not a member of this workspace Ask for membership or open the right workspace’s link

If linking succeeds but your repository still does not sync, the problem is in connections 1–3, not in your link. Give your admin the repository name, the work item key and what you expected to happen.

A first-day example

Riley joins the acme workspace. Riley’s admin sends the link https://plane.example.com/git-sync/ui/workspaces/acme/account. The card says No personal GitHub account connected. Riley selects Connect personal account, checks that GitHub shows riley-codes, and approves. Back in Plane the notice Your personal GitHub account is connected. appears.

Later that week Riley’s push contains WEB-30 #comment Draft layout pushed. The comment appears on WEB-30 under the git-sync service user, ending with “by riley-codes”. Sam, the reviewer, has their own link; Riley’s link does not map anyone else.

What you learned

  • There are four connections: App installation, installation ↔ workspace, repository ↔ project, and your personal link. Only the last one is yours.
  • Members reach My GitHub account through a direct link, because the GitHub Sync settings menu is admin-only.
  • The link stores your GitHub account’s stable numeric ID; Reconnect refreshes authorization and Disconnect personal account removes the link and the token.
  • Plane-side changes made by git-sync show the service account as author in this release; GitHub-side mirror writes can be authored as you.
  • Each OAuth error notice tells you exactly which step failed.

Source files

  • src/ui/client/Connect.tsx — the My GitHub account card, notices and buttons
  • src/ui/oauth-flow.ts — start, callback, disconnect, revoke
  • src/auth/github-user.ts — OAuth exchange, token refresh, needs_reauth
  • src/auth/identity.ts, src/app/identity.ts — sender → Plane user, email auto-match
  • src/ui/install-flow.ts — installation ↔ workspace connection
  • src/app/context.ts, src/sync/mirror.ts, src/sync/github.ts — attribution (service account, asUser)
  • packages/constants/src/settings/workspace.ts — admin-only GitHub Sync settings entry

09 · Linking branches, commits and pull requests

A work item’s key is its short address in code discussions. WEB-42 means work item 42 in the project whose identifier is WEB. When you put that key in a branch name or a pull request, git-sync links the code to the task: the PR shows up in the work item’s Development panel, a link-back comment appears on GitHub, and the team’s automation rules can move the item through its states.

This chapter explains exactly where git-sync looks for keys, how strong each kind of reference is, and how to avoid accidental links. Chapter 10 covers the magic words and WEB-NEW in detail, and chapter 11 covers commands inside commit messages.

Note: Everything here applies only to repositories an admin has mapped to a Plane project. In an unmapped repository nothing is scanned.

The key format

A key is a project prefix, a hyphen and a number:

  • The prefix starts with a letter, followed by 1–11 letters or digits (so it is 2–12 characters long): WEB, API2, MOBILEAPP.
  • The number is decimal digits. Leading zeros are dropped: WEB-0042 is WEB-42.
  • A key must not start right after a letter or digit, and must not be followed directly by a letter, digit or underscore.
Text Result
WEB-42 Key WEB-42
API2-103 Key API2-103
WEB-0042 Key WEB-42
feature/WEB-42-login Key WEB-42 (slash and following hyphen are fine boundaries)
X-42 Ignored: the prefix is only one character
WEB_42 Ignored: underscore instead of hyphen
WEB-42more Ignored: a letter follows the digits
Text Result
WEB-42_extra Ignored: an underscore follows the digits
42-WEB Ignored: wrong order

Recognizing the shape is only the first step. git-sync then asks Plane whether the work item exists in the workspace. A key with the right shape that does not exist (for example WEB-999) is not linked; see Unknown keys below.

Prefixes that are never keys

Some technical abbreviations look like keys (SHA-256, UTF-8, RFC-7231). git-sync ignores these prefixes everywhere, even after a magic word:

UTF, SHA, ISO, AES, RSA, CVE, CWE, RFC, TLS, SSL, MD, ES, PEP, USB, HTTP, IPV, SSH, GPT, RS, CRC, UTC, WIN.

If your project’s identifier is one of these, its keys will never link. Ask an admin to choose a different project identifier.

Where git-sync looks

Different places are scanned with different rules. Two properties matter: whether a bare key (one without a magic word in front) must be uppercase, and what tier a bare key gets.

Where Bare key must be uppercase? Tier of a bare key Used for
PR head branch name (the branch with your changes) No — web-42-fix works Closing PR links; branch pushes
PR title Yes Closing PR links
PR body (description) Yes Relation PR links
Commit message Yes Relation Smart Commits and push rules only — never PR links
A key right after a magic word (anywhere above) No — Refs web-42 works The magic word’s tier As for the place it appears

Some practical consequences:

  • The PR handler reads only the head branch, the title and the body. It does not read the PR’s commits. A key that appears only in a commit message never links the PR to the item. Put the key in the branch name or the PR itself.
  • The base branch (where the PR merges into, such as main) is never scanned for keys. Admin rules can inspect the base branch (for example “merged into staging”), but that is a condition, not a reference.
  • The scan is plain text. Markdown code blocks, quotes and links are still text: a pasted example containing WEB-99 in a PR body creates a relation to WEB-99.
Branch:   feature/web-42-login        → WEB-42, closing
Title:    WEB-42 Improve login        → WEB-42, closing
Title:    web-42 Improve login        → nothing (bare lowercase in a title)
Body:     Related discussion WEB-42   → WEB-42, relation
Body:     Related discussion web-42   → nothing (bare lowercase in a body)
Body:     Refs web-42                 → WEB-42, non-closing (magic word)
Commit:   WEB-42 tidy CSS             → push rules only; no PR link
Text Where Result (real parser) Why
WEB-42-checkout-button branch WEB-42 (closing) bare key in a branch
feature/web-42-login branch WEB-42 (closing) branch keys are case-insensitive
WEB-42 Keep the checkout button visible title WEB-42 (closing) bare key in a PR title
Closes WEB-42 body WEB-42 (closing) closing magic word
Refs WEB-41 body WEB-41 (non-closing) non-closing magic word
Relates to WEB-40 body WEB-40 (relation) relation magic word
See WEB-40 for context body WEB-40 (relation) bare uppercase key in a body
Closes WEB-42, WEB-43 and API2-7 body WEB-42 (closing); WEB-43 (closing); API2-7 (closing) several keys after one word
Closes: WEB-42 body WEB-42 (closing) optional colon, then a space
Text Where Result (real parser) Why
Closes:WEB-42 body WEB-42 (relation) no space after the colon: only the bare key counts
X-42 WEB_42 WEB-42more 42-WEB body no reference not keys
UTF-8 SHA-256 CVE-2024 body no reference deny-listed prefixes
Closes WEB-42⏎skip WEB-42 body skipped: WEB-42 skip removes the key from this parse

The three tiers

Each reference has a tier, which says how much automation it allows. The tier is separate from the work item’s state; it decides which rule actions may change that state.

Tier Plain meaning Typical wording Can automation change the item’s state?
Closing This code finishes the item Closes WEB-42, a key in the branch or title Yes, including the “merged” step — but only when every linked PR is merged or closed (the merge guard, chapter 14)
Non-closing This code is part of the work Refs WEB-42, Part of WEB-42 Yes for every step except “merged”
Relation Useful context only Relates to WEB-42, a bare key in the body Never

The gate applies only to state changes. If an admin writes a rule that also comments, adds a label or assigns someone, those actions run for every tier. All three tiers show the PR in the Development panel.

The demo run shows the difference. PR #118 says Refs WEB-41; opening it moved WEB-41 to In Progress (non-closing allows the “opened” step). PR #119 says Relates to WEB-40; WEB-40 stayed in Todo. Both items still list their PR:

When the same key appears several times, the strongest wins

git-sync collects every reference in the branch, title and body, then keeps one tier per work item: closing beats non-closing, which beats relation. If two references have the same tier, the record notes where it came from, preferring branch, then title, then body, then commit. That preference is bookkeeping only; it never makes a weaker tier win.

Warning: A bare key in the branch name is already closing. If a PR should only contribute part of an item, writing Refs WEB-42 in the body is not enough when the branch is web-42-part-one: the branch’s closing reference wins. Use a branch without the key, such as checkout-layout-part-one, and Refs WEB-42 in the title or body.

Link a pull request to a work item

Goal: a PR that shows up on WEB-42 and finishes it when merged

Before you start: the repository is mapped to the project (the Development panel shows a Start work section, not “No GitHub repository is mapped to this project.”).

Steps

  1. Create your branch with the key in it. The easiest way is Copy branch name or Create branch in the work item’s Development panel (chapter 12), which gives WEB-42-make-the-checkout-button-visible-on-small-screens.
  2. Push your commits.
  3. Open the pull request on GitHub. Put the key in the title, for example WEB-42 Keep the checkout button visible on small screens. ①
  4. In the body, state the intent on its own line: Closes WEB-42. ②
  5. Check the branch, title and body for keys you did not mean to link.
  6. Create the PR, then open WEB-42 in Plane and look at Development.

Result:

  • The work item’s Development panel lists the PR under Pull requests with its status (for example OPEN · REVIEW).
  • A link titled [PR] #121 WEB-42 Keep the checkout button visible on small screens · OPEN · REVIEW is added to the item’s links in Plane.
  • If the mapping has Post link-back comments on GitHub turned on, git-sync comments on the PR once per newly linked item.
  • The team’s rules run. With the shipped defaults, opening a non-draft PR moves a closing or non-closing item to In Progress; a draft PR does the same.

The link-back comment text (verbatim from the demo run):

Linked Plane work item:
- WEB-42: http://plane.example.com/acme/projects/bb57e81d-c161-441f-b50e-907af28f08c2/issues/53486230-16eb-4c87-afc4-ffeb2339a1a9

Text git-sync posted to GitHub in the demo run.

When a PR links several items at once, the heading becomes “Linked Plane work items:” with one line per item. The comment is posted only for links that are new in that delivery, so editing the PR does not repeat it.

Screenshot needed — gh-04-pr-linkback — A PR on GitHub with git-sync's 'Linked Plane work item' comment (needs a GitHub session and a live webhook). Capture later with npm run manual:capture -- --only gh-04-pr-linkback
  • Nothing in Development → the key is lowercase in the title or body without a magic word, the key exists only in commits, or the repository is not mapped.
  • Linked, but the state did not change → the reference is a relation, or your team’s rules have no step for this event. The audit log (ask an admin) shows Automation rule matched entries.
  • Linked to the wrong item → see Removing a wrong link.

Branches

A branch name is the strongest and most convenient place for a key: it is closing, case-insensitive, and used both for PR links and for branch pushes.

When you push a new branch whose name contains a key, git-sync:

  • adds a [Branch] <branch name> link to the work item (shown under Branches in the Development panel);
  • runs the “branch pushed” rule, which by default moves the item to In Progress. A new branch never moves an item that is already completed or cancelled back to In Progress.

A good convention is key first, then a short description: WEB-42-sticky-checkout-button. The Development panel suggests the team’s configured name; see chapter 12.

Commits

A key in a commit message does two things, and only two:

  1. Smart Commits — if the line has a #command after the key, git-sync runs it (chapter 11).
  2. Push rules — an admin may write rules for push or commit.pushed_to_default events; bare uppercase keys in commit messages are their targets (as relations, so they cannot change state).

A commit message never links a PR, and there is no “Commits” list in the Development panel. To see a PR’s commits, open the PR on GitHub.

Opting out: skip and ignore

In a PR body, skip WEB-42 or ignore WEB-42 removes WEB-42 from the result of that scan, wherever else it appeared (branch, title or body). The words are case-insensitive. Each phrase covers exactly one key; skip WEB-42 WEB-43 skips only WEB-42.

Closes WEB-42

This replaces the approach from WEB-17's spike.
skip WEB-17

Here WEB-17 is mentioned as context but not linked.

Warning: skip only affects new scans. git-sync remembers links it has already made. Adding skip WEB-42 (or deleting the key) after the PR was linked does not remove the stored link, and later events on the PR still reach WEB-42. Use skip in the PR body before you create the PR.

skip and ignore work only in the PR body. In a title or branch they are ordinary words.

Unknown keys

If a reference has the right shape but no such work item exists in the workspace, nothing is linked. git-sync records Work item reference not found in the audit log. When the mapping has Report problems as comments on GitHub and Plane turned on, and the PR’s sender is a linked member of the workspace, git-sync also comments once on the PR (the comment is edited in place, not repeated):

WEB-99 does not match a work item in the linked Plane workspace, so this pull request is not linked to it.

The report is limited to linked members on purpose: otherwise anyone who can open a PR could probe which keys exist in your Plane workspace.

Removing a wrong link

There is no button for developers to remove a link that git-sync has stored. Editing the PR text does not remove it either. If a PR is linked to the wrong item:

  1. Tell your workspace admin the PR URL and the wrong key, before the PR is merged.
  2. Meanwhile, avoid closing words for that key. A wrong closing link can move the wrong item to Done on merge.

One PR, several items; several PRs, one item

One PR, several items. State the intent per item on separate lines:

Closes WEB-42
Refs WEB-43
Relates to API-9

WEB-42 can complete on merge, WEB-43 moves along but does not complete, and API-9 only shows the PR. Check that the branch and title do not contain a closing key for WEB-43 or API-9.

Several PRs, one item. Each PR links on its own. The merge guard decides when the item may complete: at least one linked PR merged and none still open (chapter 14).

What you learned

  • Keys look like WEB-42; a fixed deny-list (SHA, UTF, RFC …) is never treated as keys.
  • PR links come from the head branch (any case, closing), the PR title (uppercase, closing) and the PR body (uppercase, relation). Commits never link PRs.
  • Tiers gate state changes: closing can complete on merge, non-closing moves but never completes, relation never changes state. The strongest tier per key wins.
  • skip KEY / ignore KEY in the PR body prevents a link, but cannot remove one that already exists.
  • Link-back comments and unknown-key reports appear on GitHub only when the mapping enables them.

Source files

  • src/parse/references.ts — key format, deny-list, scan rules, tiers, skip/ignore, -NEW
  • src/parse/magicWords.ts — default magic words and tier order
  • src/app/pr.ts — PR handler: sources scanned, stored links, link-back comment, unknown-key report
  • src/app/push.ts — branch link on first push, Smart Commits, push rules
  • src/app/rules.ts, src/github/pr-automation.ts — tier gating of set_state
  • tests/parse/references.test.ts

10 · Magic words and WEB-NEW

A magic word is a short phrase in front of a key that says how the code relates to the task: “this finishes it”, “this is part of it”, or “this is related”. You already met the three tiers in chapter 9. Magic words are how you choose a tier deliberately, instead of relying on where a bare key happens to appear.

This chapter lists the shipped magic words, the exact grammar, how admins can change the lists, and the special WEB-NEW marker that creates a new work item from a pull request.

Note: Magic words and Smart Commits are different tools. Closes WEB-42 in a PR describes a relationship that rules act on later (for example on merge). WEB-42 #done in a commit message is a command that runs when the commit is pushed. See chapter 11.

The default magic words

These are the lists git-sync ships with (src/parse/magicWords.ts). Your instance admin can replace them; the God mode Magic words section shows the current lists.

Tier Default phrases
Closing (20) close, closes, closed, closing, fix, fixes, fixed, fixing, resolve, resolves, resolved, resolving, complete, completes, completed, completing, implement, implements, implemented, implementing
Non-closing (7) ref, refs, references, part of, contributes to, toward, towards
Relation (2) relates to, related to

Words that are not on the list, such as see, addresses or for, are just text. The key after them is then treated as a bare key, with the tier that its location gives it (closing in a branch or title, relation in a body).

Grammar

A magic word matches when all of these hold:

  1. The phrase is a separate word: no letter, digit or underscore directly before or after it. unfixes WEB-42 does not contain the magic word fixes.
  1. The phrase is case-insensitive: CLOSES, Closes and closes are the same. Words in multi-word phrases may be separated by any whitespace (part of).
  2. An optional colon may follow the phrase.
  3. At least one whitespace character must come before the key. Closes: WEB-42 works; Closes:WEB-42 does not, because there is no space after the colon.
  4. The key right after the phrase is case-insensitive: Refs web-42 links WEB-42.

One phrase can cover several keys. Separate them with a comma, and, , and, & or plain whitespace:

Fixes WEB-42, WEB-43 and API-9
Refs WEB-42 WEB-43
Relates to WEB-42 & API-9
Closes: WEB-42

Anything else between the phrase and a key breaks the phrase. In Refs (WEB-42) the parenthesis stops the phrase; WEB-42 is then a bare key, and its tier depends on where it is.

Tier Default words and phrases (from src/parse/magicWords.ts)
closing close, closes, closed, closing, fix, fixes, fixed, fixing, resolve, resolves, resolved, resolving, complete, completes, completed, completing, implement, implements, implemented, implementing
non-closing ref, refs, references, part of, contributes to, toward, towards
relation relates to, related to

Example: Closes:WEB-42 in a PR title still links WEB-42 as closing, but only because a bare uppercase key in a title is closing anyway. The same text in a PR body is just a bare key: a relation. This is a common surprise. Always put a space after the colon.

Same key, several phrases

When a key is mentioned with different strengths, the strongest wins (closing > non-closing > relation). If the branch is web-42-login and the body says Refs WEB-42, the item is linked as closing because of the branch. A key that is already classified by a magic word is not counted a second time as a bare key: a title containing only Refs WEB-42 stays non-closing.

Choosing the right word

You want to say Write Effect with the shipped rules
This PR finishes the task Closes WEB-42 (or the key in the branch/title) Item moves to In Progress when the PR opens, In Review when review is requested, Done when merged into main
This PR is one part of the task Refs WEB-42 / Part of WEB-42 Item moves along with the PR, but merge never marks it Done
This PR is only related Relates to WEB-42 Item shows the PR in Development; its state never changes
Do not link this key at all skip WEB-42 in the PR body No link from this scan
There is no task yet WEB-NEW in the PR title or body git-sync creates the task (below)

Tip: Split work across lines so every key’s intent is visible to reviewers: Closes WEB-42 / Refs WEB-43 / Relates to API-9.

How admins change the lists

Admin only: In God mode → GitHub Sync → Magic words there is one box per tier, one phrase per line, saved with Save magic words. The lists apply to the whole instance.

The validator refuses lists that would be ambiguous or unsafe:

  • phrases must be lowercase letters and single spaces only, at most 40 characters;
  • each tier must have between 1 and 100 phrases;
  • a phrase may appear in only one tier. Otherwise saving fails with a message such as "refs" is in both closing and non_closing.

When your instance has custom words, the defaults in this chapter no longer apply. If you are unsure, ask the admin for the current lists, or check the Magic words screenshot in chapter 23.

Create a work item from a pull request: WEB-NEW

Sometimes the code comes first: a quick fix, a dependency bump, a refactor someone asked for in a hallway. If your team accepts PR-first work, put <PROJECT>-NEW in the PR title or body. git-sync creates a new work item in that project and links the PR to it.

Goal: create and link a new WEB item from a PR

Before you start: the repository is mapped to the project whose identifier you use (here WEB). Your team agrees PR-first items are acceptable.

Steps

  1. Open a pull request whose title or body contains WEB-NEW. For example, title WEB-NEW Add rate limiting to the sign-up form. ①
  2. Create the PR (or edit or reopen an existing one: the marker is checked on opened, edited and reopened events).
  3. Open the Plane project. A new work item has appeared.

Result: in the demo run, PR #122 created WEB-46:

What git-sync does:

  • The new item’s name is the PR title, exactly as written (in the demo: “WEB-NEW Add rate limiting to the sign-up form”). Rename it in Plane afterwards if you like; the link stays.
  • The item starts in a state from the project’s started group (In Progress in the demo project).
  • The PR is linked to the item with a closing link, so merging can complete it like any other closing PR.
  • The PR body is not copied into the item’s description.
  • Repeated deliveries of the same PR do not create duplicates: one item per PR and project.

Rules for the marker:

  • NEW must be uppercase. The project part may be any case: web-NEW works, WEB-new does not.
  • Only the PR title and body are scanned; a branch called WEB-NEW-… or a commit message with WEB-NEW creates nothing.
  • Prefixes on the deny-list (SHA-NEW, RFC-NEW …) are ignored.
  • If no project has that identifier, nothing is created and the audit log records the failure (“no Plane project has the identifier …”).

Warning: Known defect in this release: for an item created by WEB-NEW, the link-back comment on GitHub names the project instead of the new key. The demo run posted:

Linked Plane work item:
- WEB: http://plane.example.com/acme/projects/bb57e81d-c161-441f-b50e-907af28f08c2/issues/50b5ef6b-6077-4578-a943-8bb8db2d6cc9

The URL points to the right item (WEB-46). Only the label is wrong. This is listed in Appendix E.

Tip: WEB-NEW names a project, not a number. If the task already exists, use its real key instead; otherwise you end up with a duplicate.

Worked examples

Each row shows what the shipped word lists make of a piece of text, and where the text appears. “Bare” means the key is read without a magic word.

Text Where Result
Fixes WEB-42 PR body WEB-42, closing
FIXES web-42 PR body WEB-42, closing (phrase and key are case-insensitive)
Completing: WEB-42 PR body WEB-42, closing
Text Where Result
Part of WEB-42 PR title WEB-42, non-closing (the phrase wins over the bare-title rule for this occurrence)
Contributes to WEB-42 and API-9 PR body WEB-42 and API-9, both non-closing
Related to WEB-42, WEB-43 PR body WEB-42 and WEB-43, both relation
Closes:WEB-42 PR body WEB-42, relation (phrase does not match; bare uppercase key in a body)
Closes:WEB-42 PR title WEB-42, closing (bare uppercase key in a title)
Refs (WEB-42) PR body WEB-42, relation (parenthesis breaks the phrase)
unfixes WEB-42 PR body WEB-42, relation (fixes is not a separate word)
See WEB-42 PR body WEB-42, relation (see is not a magic word)
Addresses WEB-42 PR title WEB-42, closing (bare key in a title)
refs web-42 PR body WEB-42, non-closing
web-42 PR body nothing (bare lowercase)
Fixes SHA-256 anywhere nothing (deny-listed prefix)
Refs WEB-42 with branch web-42-part-one PR WEB-42, closing (the branch is stronger)

The generated tables in Appendix C run every such example through the real parser, so they always match the code.

Example: A reviewer asks why WEB-43 moved to Done although the PR said Refs WEB-43. The title was WEB-42 WEB-43 Checkout fixes. Bare keys in a title are closing, and the strongest tier wins, so both items were closing. Writing the title without WEB-43 would have kept it non-closing.

A preview of the merge guard

Closing words have one more safety net. When a PR merges, a closing item moves to Done only if at least one linked PR has merged and none is still open. A PR that was closed without merging neither blocks nor counts. If another linked PR cannot be read from GitHub, git-sync treats it as open, to be safe.

The guard is evaluated only at the moment of a merge. If WEB-36 has two PRs, merging the first one does not complete it (the second is open), and later closing the second PR without merging does not re-run the check. Close obsolete PRs before the final merge, or move the item by hand. Chapter 14 shows this with screenshots.

What you learned

  • There are 20 closing, 7 non-closing and 2 relation phrases by default; admins can replace them per instance.
  • A phrase is case-insensitive, may have a colon, and needs whitespace before the key (Closes: WEB-42, not Closes:WEB-42).
  • One phrase can cover several keys separated by commas, and, & or spaces.
  • WEB-NEW in a PR title or body creates a work item named after the PR title, in a started state, linked as closing.
  • Closing words complete an item only when the merge guard passes.

  • src/app/pr.ts — createRequested (WEB-NEW), merge guard input (otherPrStates)
  • src/github/pr-automation.ts — merge guard on set_state
