21 · Install git-sync

This chapter takes you from a running Plane to a running git-sync. You prepare three things in Plane: a service account, its API key and a webhook. Then you run one command, ./install.sh, on the Plane server. The GitHub side comes afterwards, in chapters 22–24.

Overview

Step Where Time Who
1. Create a service account Plane sign-up + Workspace settings → Members 5 min Workspace admin
2. Create its API key Plane, signed in as the service account 2 min Workspace admin
3. Allow the internal webhook host plane.env on the server 5 min Server operator
4. Create the Plane webhook Workspace settings → Webhooks 2 min Workspace admin
5. Run ./install.sh Server shell 5 min, plus 10–20 min for the first UI build Server operator
6. Fix framing if the page is blank Your proxy as needed Server operator

Step 1 — Create a separate service account

Goal: give git-sync its own Plane identity

Before you start: decide on an email address for the bot. It must be a different Plane user from every person.

Warning: Do not use your own account. git-sync ignores Plane changes made by its service account, because they look like its own echoes. If the service account is you, your own edits never sync to GitHub. The installer prints this reminder too: “git-sync ignores Plane changes made by this account (they look like its own). Use a dedicated account, not your personal one, or your own edits will not sync to GitHub.”

Steps

  1. In a private browser window, open your Plane sign-in page and choose Sign up (if your instance allows self-registration). Create the user, for example display name GitHub Bot.
  2. Back in your admin session, open Workspace settings → Members and invite the bot to every workspace you will sync.
  3. Accept the invitation in the bot’s session.
  4. Join the bot to the projects you will map, so it can read and update their work items.

Result: the bot is a member of the workspace and its projects.

If it went wrong:

  • Sign up is not offered → self-registration is disabled. Ask the instance admin to create the user through the instance’s normal account process.
  • A Gmail address is the only one available → a plus address such as you+gitsync@example.com is a distinct Plane user that still delivers to your mailbox. Use it only if your instance accepts it, and double-check you are signed in as the bot before step 2.

Step 2 — Create the service account’s API key

Goal: a Plane Personal Access Token owned by the bot

Before you start: be signed in as the bot, not as yourself. A token made in your session belongs to you, whatever its title says.

Steps

  1. Open the bot’s avatar menu and choose Settings.
  2. Choose Personal Access Tokens.
  3. Select Add access token, enter a title such as git-sync bot, choose an expiry, and generate the token.
  4. Copy the token into a safe temporary place. You will paste it into the installer’s hidden prompt.

Result: you have a token. The installer verifies it against Plane (/api/v1/users/me/) and records the bot’s user ID by itself. You never type that ID.

If it went wrong: an expired or revoked token stops all Plane writes. Put a reminder in your calendar before the expiry date; rotation is in chapter 29.

Step 3 — Allow Plane to send webhooks to git-sync

Goal: git-sync.internal in Plane’s webhook allow-list

Plane refuses webhooks to its own public domain and to host names without a dot. git-sync therefore receives Plane’s webhooks inside Docker under the alias git-sync.internal, which the installer adds to Plane’s network. Plane only sends to it if the name is in WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

Steps (on the server, in Plane’s directory)

  1. Open Plane’s env file (often plane.env).
  2. Set WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS=git-sync.internal, or append ,git-sync.internal if the variable already has a value.
  3. Apply it to the running API with your usual full Compose command, for example:
docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml --env-file plane.env up -d api worker beat-worker

Use up -d, not restart: restart keeps the old environment.

Result: the running api container has the new value. The installer reads it from the running container, not from the file, and stops if it is missing:

Plane does not allow webhooks to git-sync yet. Add git-sync.internal to WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS in Plane's env file
  (e.g. WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS=git-sync.internal, or append ,git-sync.internal to an existing value),
  restart Plane's api, worker and beat-worker with your usual compose command, then run ./install.sh again.
  Nothing has been changed yet.

Step 4 — Create the Plane webhook

Goal: Plane sends every workspace change to git-sync

Before you start: Step 3 is applied. Do this once per workspace you will sync.

Steps

  1. Open Workspace settings → Webhooks and select Add webhook.
  2. URL: http://git-sync.internal:3100/git-sync/webhooks/plane (exactly this; http, port 3100).
  3. Choose Send me everything.
  4. Save, then copy the secret key Plane shows. Keep it with the bot token.

Result: the webhook exists. Until git-sync is running, Plane cannot deliver to it; keep the gap short. Plane switches a webhook off after about 30–50 minutes of failed connections (chapter 29 explains how to re-enable it).

If it went wrong:

Message in Plane Cause Fix
“Webhook not created” / URL refused You used your Plane domain, or a name without a dot, or git-sync.internal is not in the running WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS Use the exact internal URL; repeat step 3 with up -d

Note: The Plane webhook secret, the bot’s API key and (later) the GitHub webhook secret are three different secrets. Never substitute one for another.

Step 5 — Run the installer

Goal: git-sync running and healthy next to Plane

Before you start:

  • A shell on the server that runs Plane.
  • The bot token and the Plane webhook secret.
  • Docker access for your user. Use sudo only if root owns the Docker daemon Plane runs on. With rootless Docker, run as the owning user.

Steps

  1. Get the code and enter it:
git clone https://github.com/nathanabay/git_plane-intergration.git git-sync
cd git-sync
  1. Start the installer:
sudo ./install.sh
  1. Answer the prompts (typed secrets are hidden):
Prompt (exact text) Shown when Enter
Start Plane now and install git-sync on it? [Y/n] Plane is installed but stopped Y only if this is the Plane you mean
Plane API key of the git-sync service account: First install, or the stored key was rejected The bot token from step 2
Plane webhook secret: First install The secret from step 4
Public URL of your Plane site (e.g. https://plane.example.com): Plane’s WEB_URL could not be read Your public Plane address
GitHub App webhook secret: Only with --github-app-id and --github-private-key The App’s webhook secret (chapter 22)
  1. Wait. The installer prints one heading per stage:
Heading What happens
==> Checking Docker and Plane Finds Docker, Compose and Plane (running, stopped, or only its folder). Reproduces how Plane was started and refuses if it cannot.
==> Building the git-sync image Builds git-sync:local from this checkout.
==> Preparing the Plane UI images (adds Git Sync to Plane's menus) On Plane v1.4.2 only: builds plane-frontend-gitsync:v1.4.2 and plane-admin-gitsync:v1.4.2 (first time: often 10–20 minutes), or reuses them.
==> Configuring git-sync Checks the bot token, checks WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS, writes git-sync.env, creates the gitsync database and role, patches the proxy route, merges the Compose override.
==> Starting git-sync Validates the merged Compose model, runs up -d, waits up to 2 minutes for /git-sync/healthz, checks the proxy answers.

Result: the installer ends with git-sync is installed. and prints the next steps. It also prints the command you must use from now on to start Plane:

Start Plane with this command from now on, so git-sync is included (Plane's setup.sh leaves it out):
    cd /root/plane && docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml -f docker-compose.override.yaml --env-file plane.env up -d

Warning: Plane’s own setup.sh start/restart ignores the override file, so it starts Plane without git-sync. Copy the printed command into your runbook and use it instead.

All installer options

Option Use it when
--plane-dir DIR More than one Plane runs on the machine (“Found more than one Plane. Choose one with --plane-dir DIR”), or Plane is in an unusual folder
--env-file FILE The installer cannot tell which env file Plane was started with (“Could not work out how this Plane was started”)
--public-url URL Plane’s WEB_URL is not the address people actually use
--keep-plane-ui Keep Plane’s stock web/admin images and skip the slow UI build. git-sync pages stay reachable at <url>/git-sync/ui/admin and <url>/git-sync/ui/workspaces/<slug>
--with-plane-ui Always use the git-sync Plane UI images (the default on v1.4.2 is automatic)
--proxy plane Default: route /git-sync/* through Plane’s own proxy
--proxy external --gateway-network NAME Your own reverse proxy serves Plane. git-sync joins that Docker network as git-sync; add the route yourself (see below)
Option Use it when
--github-app-id ID --github-private-key FILE Enter the GitHub App at install time instead of in God mode. The two go together; the webhook secret is asked for
-y, --yes Scripted install: never prompt. Secrets come from GITSYNC_PLANE_PAT, GITSYNC_PLANE_WEBHOOK_SECRET and GITSYNC_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET; the public URL from GITSYNC_PUBLIC_ORIGIN
--uninstall Remove git-sync from Plane, keeping its database and settings (chapter 29)
--purge With --uninstall: also delete git-sync’s database and settings
-h, --help Show the help

Example: your own Caddy serves Plane over a Docker network called gateway.

sudo ./install.sh --plane-dir /root/plane --proxy external --gateway-network gateway

The installer then prints the route to add to your proxy, placed before the Plane route:

handle /git-sync/* {
    reverse_proxy git-sync:3100
}

Example: scripted install without prompts.

read -r -s -p 'Bot PAT: ' GITSYNC_PLANE_PAT; export GITSYNC_PLANE_PAT
read -r -s -p 'Plane webhook secret: ' GITSYNC_PLANE_WEBHOOK_SECRET; export GITSYNC_PLANE_WEBHOOK_SECRET
sudo --preserve-env=GITSYNC_PLANE_PAT,GITSYNC_PLANE_WEBHOOK_SECRET ./install.sh -y
unset GITSYNC_PLANE_PAT GITSYNC_PLANE_WEBHOOK_SECRET

With -y, a missing answer is an error that names the variable. The installer never invents a secret.

Note: The non-interactive error for the webhook secret mentions a --plane-webhook-secret flag. install.sh has no such flag; set GITSYNC_PLANE_WEBHOOK_SECRET instead (logged in manual/notes/discrepancies.md).

What the installer changes on the server

Item Change
docker-compose.override.yaml Adds the git-sync service (and, with UI forks, web/admin image entries). Your own entries, comments and !override/!reset tags are kept. Backed up first as .bak-<time>.
git-sync.env Created, mode 0600, owner-only. Existing values and extra keys are kept on re-runs. Backed up first.
git-sync/ Private directory for the optional App key and the credential-state marker (owned by UID 1000).
Postgres A gitsync role and gitsync database on Plane’s database server. Plane’s own database is untouched.
Proxy (bundled mode) A patched Caddyfile with reverse_proxy /git-sync/* git-sync:3100 before Plane’s catch-all, mounted into proxy. Refuses if your proxy already mounts its own Caddyfile.
Generated values Database password, GITSYNC_TOKEN_KEY (32 random bytes, base64), PUBLIC_ORIGIN, PLANE_API_RATE_PER_MINUTE (read from Plane’s API_KEY_RATE_LIMIT), PLANE_SERVICE_USER_ID

Is it safe on a live Plane?

  • No change unless Plane can be reproduced. The installer only touches Plane’s containers if it can rebuild exactly how Plane was started. It compares Compose’s configuration hash for api and plane-db with the running containers; if they differ, it stops before changing anything.
  • Plane’s own services are not recreated. Only the proxy and, with the UI images, the web and admin apps restart.
  • Backups first. Changed files are backed up next to themselves before each change.
  • Plane’s data is never touched. git-sync uses its own database and role; --purge drops only those.
  • Secrets are never printed. Do not run the installer with bash -x, which would print them.
  • Existing override files are flagged. If an existing override file was not loaded when Plane started, the installer warns: “…exists but the running Plane was started without it; its other entries will now apply too”.

Step 6 — Blank GitHub Sync page? Fix framing

Plane shows git-sync inside an iframe. git-sync allows framing by the same origin (frame-ancestors 'self'). If your reverse proxy adds X-Frame-Options: DENY or Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' to every response, the embedded page stays blank.

Goal: the embedded page loads

Steps

  1. Open https://<your Plane>/git-sync/ui/admin in its own tab. If it loads there but not inside Plane, framing is the problem.
  2. Exclude /git-sync/* from the blanket header. Caddy:
plane.example.com {
    handle /git-sync/* {
        header -X-Frame-Options
        reverse_proxy git-sync:3100
    }
    handle {
        header X-Frame-Options DENY
        reverse_proxy plane-proxy:80
    }
}

nginx:

location /git-sync/ {
    proxy_pass http://git-sync:3100;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_hide_header X-Frame-Options;
}
location / {
    proxy_pass http://plane-proxy:80;
    add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always;
}
  1. Validate and reload the proxy, then reload the Plane page.

Result: GitHub Sync shows the git-sync page inside Plane.

If it went wrong: check every proxy layer (CDN, outer proxy, Plane proxy). One layer adding a denial is enough to block the frame. Keep git-sync’s own frame-ancestors 'self': do not remove all CSP.

Check the installation

curl -i https://plane.example.com/git-sync/healthz

The answer is 200 with {"status":"ok"}. This only proves the HTTP service answers. Next, open God mode → GitHub Sync and look at Connection health and Setup checks (chapter 23).

Troubleshooting the installer

Message Cause Fix
Docker is not installed. / Cannot talk to the Docker daemon. No Docker or no permission Install Docker; use sudo or the right rootless user
The Docker Compose plugin is missing Old Docker Install the Compose plugin
Plane is not installed here (no Plane found in Docker or in the usual folders). No Plane found Install Plane first, or pass --plane-dir
Found more than one Plane. Choose one with --plane-dir DIR Several Plane projects Pass --plane-dir
Could not work out how this Plane was started (which env file it uses). Env file not detected Pass --env-file /path/plane.env
Running Plane with --env-file … does not reproduce the running Plane; check the file Wrong env file Use the file Plane really runs with; never bypass
Plane's directory … is not writable by this user (try sudo) Permissions Run as the owner or with sudo
Plane rejected the API key Expired, revoked or wrong token Make a new bot token; run GITSYNC_PLANE_PAT=<key> sudo -E ./install.sh or answer the re-prompt
Plane does not allow webhooks to git-sync yet… Step 3 not applied Add git-sync.internal, up -d api worker beat-worker
Plane's proxy service is not running. If you use your own reverse proxy, pass --proxy external External proxy Use --proxy external
Message Cause Fix
could not read the Caddyfile from Plane's proxy image; use --proxy external / proxy already mounts its own Caddyfile Custom proxy Use --proxy external and add the route yourself
building plane-…-gitsync:v1.4.2 failed (re-run, or use --keep-plane-ui) UI build failed (network, disk) Re-run, or --keep-plane-ui
the merged compose configuration is invalid (a backup of the override was kept next to it) Override conflict Inspect the override and its .bak- file
git-sync did not become healthy within 2 minutes (logs above) Start failure Read the printed logs; docker compose logs git-sync
GitHub App ID must be a number / --github-app-id and --github-private-key go together Bad App options Pass both, numeric ID, readable PEM
Installer stops with no message Shell error, lost terminal, Docker failure Note the exit code, check Docker context and logs, re-run interactively (never with bash -x)

What you learned

  • Prepare a dedicated service account, its API key, the git-sync.internal allow-list entry and a Plane webhook to http://git-sync.internal:3100/git-sync/webhooks/plane first.
  • ./install.sh finds Plane, proves it can reproduce it, builds images, writes git-sync.env, creates its own database, routes /git-sync/* and waits for health.
  • Every option, prompt and message, and how to run it non-interactively with -y.
  • Always start Plane afterwards with the printed full Compose command.
  • A blank embedded page is a proxy framing header; exclude /git-sync/*.

Source files

  • install.sh — host-side installer and options
  • src/install/main.ts, plane-env.ts, plane-api.ts, env-file.ts, compose.ts, caddy.ts, database.ts — container-side configuration
  • INSTALL.md, deploy/APPLY.md — installation reference and runbook
  • src/ui/static.ts — UI security headers (frame-ancestors 'self')

22 · Register the GitHub App

git-sync talks to GitHub as a GitHub App: a named integration with an explicit list of permissions and events. You register it once per instance on the GitHub account or organization that will own it. Then you install it on the repositories you want to sync. This chapter covers registration and the six values you copy into God mode. Installation and connection to a workspace are in chapter 24.

Note: No GitHub session was available when this manual was produced, so GitHub’s own forms are shown as Illustrations plus placeholders for real screenshots. The values and choices below come from the code (src/ui/setup-check.ts, src/github/hosts.ts) and the runbook.

Three different things on GitHub

Thing What it is Where you do it
Register the App Create the App definition: name, URLs, permissions, events, keys GitHub Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App (for an organization: the organization’s settings)
Install the App Give the App access to an account’s repositories From git-sync’s Connect GitHub button (chapter 24) or the App’s public page
Authorize your personal account Let git-sync know who you are on GitHub Connect personal account in git-sync (chapter 8)

Before you start

  • Your Plane public address, for example https://plane.example.com. Use the address people actually visit, with no trailing path and no invented port.
  • Permission to create a GitHub App on the owning account or organization.
  • A private shell where you can create a random secret:
openssl rand -hex 32

Keep the output private. It is the webhook secret, and you will enter it on GitHub and in God mode.

Register the App

Goal: a GitHub App with git-sync’s URLs, permissions and events

Screenshot needed — gh-01-new-app-form — GitHub's New GitHub App form (organization settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App), filled with the values below, not submitted, Client ID/slug masked. Capture later with npm run manual:capture -- --only gh-01-new-app-form

Steps

  1. Open New GitHub App on the owning account or organization.
  2. Fill in General:
Field Value Why
GitHub App name A unique, recognizable name, e.g. Acme Plane Sync Shown on installations and on comments the App posts (<slug>[bot])
Homepage URL https://plane.example.com Where the integration is used
Callback URL https://plane.example.com/git-sync/oauth/github/callback Returns people after Connect personal account
Expire user authorization tokens Leave on (GitHub’s default) git-sync stores expiry and refreshes tokens; a failed refresh asks the member to Reconnect
Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation Off When on, GitHub hides the Setup URL and sends installers to the OAuth callback instead
Enable Device Flow Off Not used
Setup URL https://plane.example.com/git-sync/install/github/callback Returns an App installation to the right Plane workspace
Redirect on update On Returns to git-sync after someone changes the installation’s repository selection
  1. Fill in Webhook:
Field Value
Active On
Webhook URL https://plane.example.com/git-sync/webhooks/github
Webhook secret The value from openssl rand -hex 32
SSL verification Enabled
  1. Set Permissions exactly as below. git-sync’s setup check compares the App registration against this list (REQUIRED_APP_PERMISSIONS):
Scope Permission Access Why git-sync needs it
Repository Pull requests Read and write Read PR lifecycle; post link-back comments on PRs
Repository Issues Read and write Mirror issues: fields, labels, assignees, comments
Repository Contents Read and write Read commits and branches; Create branch from the Development panel
Repository Checks Read Build results (check suites and runs)
Repository Commit statuses Read Combined status (ready for merge) and the status event
Repository Deployments Read Deployment results and preview URLs
Repository Metadata Read Repository identity and installation checks (always required by GitHub)
Scope Permission Access Why git-sync needs it
Organization Members Read Prove an organization owner/admin when connecting an organization installation

Checks and Commit statuses are separate permissions; choosing one does not grant the other. Leave everything else at No access.

Note: The runbook also lists Administration: Read and write for GitHub autolink references. The mapping form shows GitHub autolink references (unavailable) in this release, so do not grant it.

  1. Under Subscribe to events, tick these nine events (REQUIRED_APP_EVENTS):
Event on GitHub’s form git-sync uses it for
Pull request Linking, lifecycle rules, Development panel
Pull request review Review badges, approved / changes requested, ready for merge
Push Smart Commits, branch created, branch links
Issues Issue mirroring
Issue comment Mirrored comments
Check suite Build status, ready for merge
Check run Build status
Status Commit status (legacy CI)
Deployment status Deployments and previews

installation and installation_repositories events arrive automatically; you cannot and need not tick them.

  1. Where can this GitHub App be installed?

    • Choose Only on this account if all repositories belong to the App’s owner.
    • Choose Any account if other accounts or organizations will install it.
    • This choice does not grant access to any repository by itself.

  2. Select Create GitHub App.

Screenshot needed — gh-02-app-permissions — the created App's "Permissions & events" page showing the eight permissions and nine events, secrets/IDs masked. Capture later with npm run manual:capture -- --only gh-02-app-permissions

Collect the six values

On the App’s settings page:

Value Where on GitHub Looks like Goes to God mode field
App ID “About” section A number, e.g. 1234567 App ID
Value Where on GitHub Looks like Goes to God mode field
Client ID “About” section Text starting with Iv on GitHub.com (an OAuth App’s Ov… ID is the wrong kind of registration) OAuth client ID
App slug The last part of the App’s public link https://github.com/apps/<slug> e.g. acme-plane-sync App slug
Client secret Generate a new client secret Shown once OAuth client secret
Private key Generate a private key — a .pem file downloads -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----… Private key (PEM) (paste the file’s contents)
Webhook secret You generated it 64 hex characters Webhook secret

The App ID and the Client ID are different values and cannot be swapped. The slug is a URL name, not the numeric ID.

Secret Authenticates
Private key The App itself (JWT and installation tokens)
Client secret Personal account authorization (OAuth code exchange)
Webhook secret Incoming GitHub events

Keep all three private. If GitHub no longer shows a secret, generate a new one rather than trying to recover it.

Next: enter the values in God mode (chapter 23, “Enter the GitHub App”).

GitHub Enterprise

The same three git-sync URLs are used with GitHub Enterprise. Register the App on that GitHub host: a GitHub.com App cannot be installed on an unrelated Enterprise Server.

Edition (God mode GitHub edition) Extra field API base Web/OAuth/install origin
GitHub.com — https://api.github.com https://github.com
Enterprise Cloud with data residency Enterprise Cloud subdomain, e.g. octocorp (“The enterprise name before .ghe.com.”) https://api.octocorp.ghe.com https://octocorp.ghe.com
Enterprise Server Enterprise Server URL, e.g. https://ghe.example.com https://ghe.example.com/api/v3 https://ghe.example.com

Changing the App later

  • Permissions or events changed on GitHub: existing installations must accept the new permissions (GitHub asks the owner). God mode’s App permissions check reads the registration, not the installation’s acceptance. Ask owners to approve, then press Refresh connection in the workspace.
  • A new private key, client secret or webhook secret: save it in God mode with the other secret fields left empty. For the webhook secret, change GitHub and God mode close together, then redeliver any failed deliveries from Advanced → Recent deliveries (chapter 29).
  • A different App (new App ID): personal tokens issued for the old App no longer work. Every member must Reconnect, and installations must be connected again.

If it went wrong

Symptom Cause Fix
GitHub: redirect_uri is not associated with this application Callback URL differs from <PUBLIC_ORIGIN>/git-sync/oauth/github/callback, or wrong Client ID Compare character by character; use the App’s Client ID
The Setup URL field is greyed out Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation is on Turn it off, then enter the Setup URL and Redirect on update
God mode App permissions: Needs attention — “The App registration is missing required permission levels…” A permission missing or too low Fix the permissions table, then owners approve
God mode App webhook events: Needs attention — “Subscribe the App to the missing webhook events.” An event not ticked Tick all nine
Signed GitHub deliveries: Not verified No GitHub event received yet, or wrong webhook URL/secret Make a PR change; check Advanced → Recent deliveries on GitHub for 401/404
Deliveries show 401 on GitHub Webhook secret differs between GitHub and God mode Save the same secret in both; redeliver
Deliveries show 503 git-sync cannot decrypt its stored secret See chapter 30, “Credentials cannot be decrypted”

What you learned

  • Register once, install per account, authorize per person — three separate GitHub steps.
  • The three URLs: /git-sync/oauth/github/callback, /git-sync/install/github/callback (with Redirect on update), /git-sync/webhooks/github.
  • Eight permissions (PRs, Issues, Contents read/write; Checks, Commit statuses, Deployments, Metadata read; Organization Members read) and nine events.
  • Six values go to God mode: App ID, Client ID, slug, client secret, private key, webhook secret.

Source files

  • src/ui/setup-check.ts — REQUIRED_APP_PERMISSIONS, REQUIRED_APP_EVENTS
  • src/github/hosts.ts — editions and derived URLs
  • src/ui/oauth-flow.ts, src/ui/install-flow.ts — callback handlers
  • deploy/APPLY.md — “GitHub App registration”

23 · God mode settings (instance admin)

Everything that applies to the whole Plane instance lives on one page, Git sync: instance settings. That includes the GitHub App credentials, the setup checks, which installation belongs to which workspace, the magic words and the defaults. Only a Plane instance administrator signed in to God mode can open it.

Open the page

  1. Open God mode on your Plane (https://<your Plane>/god-mode/) and sign in as an instance admin.
  2. Choose GitHub Sync in the sidebar (“Manage GitHub synchronization.”).

Without the UI fork (installed with --keep-plane-ui), open https://<your Plane>/git-sync/ui/admin directly. You still need a God mode session in the same browser. A normal workspace session gets Not authorised with “The instance settings need a Plane instance-admin session.”

The page has two tabs: Settings (this chapter) and Instance audit (chapter 28). The Settings tab contains, top to bottom:

Section Purpose
Connection health Is the database reachable, is an App configured, how many mappings, latest activity, recent failures
Setup checks Six read-only checks of credentials, App registration, deliveries and rate limit
GitHub App Enter or replace the App’s credentials and GitHub edition
Workspace GitHub App installations Allow-list which installation belongs to which workspace
Disabled repository mappings Mappings that cannot sync and why
Manual mapping recovery Map a repository by ID when nobody can authorize personally
Magic words The closing / non-closing / relation phrase lists
Defaults Smart Commits default, signed-commit preference, reconciliation interval, echo TTL

Connection health

Card Meaning
Database — reachable / unreachable git-sync can query its gitsync database
GitHub App — configured / not configured App credentials are stored or supplied by the environment
Repository mappings Number of mappings across all workspaces (Unknown if unreadable)
Last sync activity Most recent recorded activity
Failures in the last 24 hours Count; the link opens the instance audit filtered to errors

If the stored App secrets cannot be decrypted, a red notice appears: GitHub App credentials cannot be decrypted. Save the App secrets again. (chapter 30).

Setup checks

Setup checks runs six read-only checks when the page opens; Check setup again re-runs them. Each shows Verified, Needs attention or Not verified, with a one-line explanation. Nothing is written anywhere by running them.

Check Verified when Typical “Needs attention / Not verified” text and fix
App credentials “Active App credentials can be read and decrypted.” “No GitHub App is configured yet…” → fill GitHub App. “App credentials cannot be read or decrypted…” → see chapter 30.
App permissions “Required App registration permissions match. Verify installation approval after any permission change.” “The App registration is missing required permission levels. Update it and verify installation approval.” → fix permissions on GitHub (chapter 22)
App webhook events “Required webhook subscriptions match.” “Subscribe the App to the missing webhook events.” → tick all nine events
Check Verified when Typical “Needs attention / Not verified” text and fix
Signed GitHub deliveries “A verified transport delivery was processed or durably spooled.” “No verified transport delivery is recorded yet. Make an issue or PR change to verify the webhook.”
Plane deliveries Same as above, for Plane Same; check the Plane webhook exists and is enabled
Plane request rate “Plane’s deployment setting and this service’s request limit match.” Usually Not verified: “The client limit matches config. Confirm Plane API_KEY_RATE_LIMIT separately: Plane v1.4.2 does not expose the total limit in API response headers.” This is normal. Needs attention “The active client request limit differs from PLANE_API_RATE_PER_MINUTE. Restart with matching settings.” means the running service and its configuration disagree.

Note: App permissions and App webhook events read the App registration with the App’s own identity (GET /app). They cannot tell whether an organization owner has already accepted changed permissions on an installation. After changing permissions, also check each installation on GitHub.

Tip: “Not verified” for the two delivery checks right after installation just means nothing has happened yet. Open a PR or edit a work item, then press Check setup again.

Enter the GitHub App

Goal: git-sync can authenticate as your GitHub App

Before you start: the six values from chapter 22: App ID, private key file, webhook secret, App slug, Client ID and client secret.

Steps

  1. Scroll to GitHub App. A new instance says “No GitHub App is configured yet.”
  2. App ID — the number. ①
  3. Private key (PEM) — paste the whole contents of the downloaded .pem file, including the BEGIN/END lines. ②
  4. Webhook secret — the value you set on GitHub. ③
  5. App slug — “Used for the Connect GitHub installation link.” ④
  6. OAuth client ID and OAuth client secret — “Required for personal account authorization.” ④
  7. GitHub edition — GitHub.com, Enterprise Cloud with data residency (then Enterprise Cloud subdomain), or Enterprise Server (then Enterprise Server URL). ⑤
  8. Select Save GitHub App. ⑥

Result: the panel now says “A GitHub App is configured. Leave the secrets empty to keep the stored ones.” Secret fields say “Stored encrypted; it is never shown again.” and “Configured. Leave empty to keep the secret.” Press Check setup again; App credentials, App permissions and App webhook events should turn Verified. The running service picks up new credentials within about five seconds; no restart is needed.

If it went wrong:

  • “appId must be a positive integer” → you pasted the Client ID into App ID.
  • Connect GitHub stays disabled in workspaces (“Ask the instance admin to configure the GitHub App client ID, client secret and App slug.”) → one of slug, Client ID or client secret is missing.
  • App permissions Not verified “The App registration could not be read from GitHub…” → wrong private key, wrong App ID, wrong edition/host, or no outbound connectivity.

Admin only: Once you have saved the App in God mode, the stored credentials take precedence over any GITHUB_APP_ID / GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH / GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET bootstrap values in git-sync.env. git-sync records that the bootstrap is retired, so deleting the stored row later does not quietly revive old environment secrets.

Workspace GitHub App installations (allow-list)

“Allow-list GitHub App installations per workspace. A repository can only be mapped if its installation is allow-listed for that workspace.”

Normally a workspace admin connects an installation with Connect GitHub (chapter 24), and git-sync records it here automatically. Use this panel when:

  • you want to pre-approve an installation for a workspace,
  • an organization owner installed the App directly on GitHub, or
  • you need to move or remove an installation.

Goal: allow an installation for one workspace

Steps

  1. Find the installation’s numeric ID. On GitHub it is the number at the end of the installation’s settings URL: …/settings/installations/<id>.
  2. Under Allow-list an installation, enter Installation ID (“Numeric GitHub App installation ID.”). ②
  3. Choose Workspace (“Workspace allowed to use this installation.”).
  4. Optionally enter Account / Org (optional) (“GitHub org or user name for display.”).
  5. Select Allow-list installation.

Result: the table (Workspace, Installation ID, Account / Org, Allow-listed at) shows the entry. git-sync immediately re-checks that workspace’s mappings for the installation.

If it went wrong: “That installation is already allowed for another workspace; remove it there first” — one installation serves one workspace. Remove the other entry first (“Remove allow-list entry for installation <id>?”). Removing an entry disables every mapping that used it.

Disabled repository mappings

“Unresolved mappings and mappings whose installation is no longer allowed are disabled. Allow-list the installation for its workspace, then have a workspace admin save the mapping to verify it.”

The table lists Workspace, Repository, Project, Installation and Reason. The reasons are:

Reason Meaning Fix
Save the mapping to verify its installation (installation Unresolved) The mapping has no verified installation yet (for example, it was restored or created before the allow-list) A workspace admin opens the mapping and presses Save changes
Installation is not allowed for this workspace The installation was removed from the allow-list, uninstalled on GitHub, or moved Allow-list it again (above), or reconnect it, then save the mapping

Refresh mappings reloads the list. A disabled mapping does not sync anything. Its sync health card in the workspace says Disabled · <reason> (chapter 28).

Manual mapping recovery

“Instance admins can map a repository by ID when personal GitHub authorization is unavailable. The App installation and Plane project are still verified.”

Use this when a workspace admin cannot use the normal repository picker, for example because nobody with access can connect a personal GitHub account. It is a recovery tool; prefer Map a repository in the workspace.

Goal: map a repository without a personal GitHub link

Steps

  1. Choose Workspace. ①
  2. Choose Plane project. ②
  3. Enter GitHub repository as owner/repository, and GitHub repository ID. The ID is the repository’s numeric id from GET /repos/{owner}/{repo} on the GitHub API. ②
  4. Select Add manual mapping. ③

Result: the mapping is created with default settings: two-way, the instance’s Smart Commits default, link-back comments on, problem reports off. A workspace admin can then tune it on its Settings tab.

If it went wrong:

  • Not saved → git-sync still verifies that the repository’s installation is allow-listed for that workspace, that the App can read the repository with that ID and name, and that the project belongs to the workspace.
  • An ID and name that do not match → refused.

Magic words

The instance-wide phrases that turn a reference in a PR into a closing, non-closing or relation link (chapter 10 explains them for developers).

Box Default
Closing words close, closes, closed, closing, fix, fixes, fixed, fixing, resolve, resolves, resolved, resolving, complete, completes, completed, completing, implement, implements, implemented, implementing
Non-closing words ref, refs, references, part of, contributes to, toward, towards
Box Default
Relation phrases relates to, related to

Goal: change the vocabulary your teams use

Steps

  1. Edit the boxes: “One word or phrase per line. A word may belong to only one tier.” ①
  2. Select Save magic words. ②

Rules the save enforces:

  • Only lowercase letters and single spaces (no digits, hyphens or punctuation).
  • At most 40 characters per phrase, and 1–100 phrases per tier.
  • No tier may be empty.
  • A phrase in two tiers is refused with "<word>" is in both <tier> and <tier>.

Result: the new lists apply to the next PR event in every workspace. Existing links keep their tier.

Warning: Removing a closing word your teams use (for example fixes) silently turns Fixes WEB-42 into a bare body reference, which is only a relation. Announce changes.

Defaults

Field Default Effect
Enable Smart Commits for newly mapped repositories On Pre-ticks Smart Commits in the Map a repository form. Existing mappings are not changed.
Require signed commits for Smart Commits The value of REQUIRE_VERIFIED_COMMITS Stored but not enforced in this release. See the warning below.
Reconciliation interval (minutes) 60 “How often missed webhooks are reconciled.” Also how quickly a silent Plane webhook is noticed.
Field Default Effect
Echo-suppression TTL (minutes) 10 “How long an applied operation is remembered to stop sync loops.” Too long can swallow a genuine identical edit; too short can let an echo through.

Select Save defaults to store them.

Warning: The checkbox Require signed commits for Smart Commits (“Only commits GitHub marks as verified can run Smart Commit commands when enabled.”) is saved, but the Smart Commit push handler does not read it. It only reads the environment variable REQUIRE_VERIFIED_COMMITS (src/app/push.ts:55). To enforce signed commits:

  1. Set REQUIRE_VERIFIED_COMMITS=true in git-sync.env.
  2. Restart git-sync with the full Compose command: docker compose … up -d git-sync.

When it is on, an unsigned commit’s commands are skipped and audited. If Report problems is enabled on the mapping, git-sync posts “This commit is not signature-verified; Smart Commit commands were ignored.”

What you learned

  • God mode → GitHub Sync (/git-sync/ui/admin) holds everything instance-wide and needs a God mode session.
  • Setup checks verify credentials, App permissions, the nine events, deliveries and the rate limit, without writing anything.
  • GitHub App secrets are encrypted and write-only; leave fields blank to keep them.
  • The installation allow-list binds one installation to one workspace; removing it disables mappings, listed under Disabled repository mappings.
  • Magic words are validated strictly, and the signed-commit checkbox is not enforced — use REQUIRE_VERIFIED_COMMITS.

  • src/ui/api.ts — /instance/* routes (github-app, installations, magic-words, settings, health)
  • src/ui/validate.ts — parseGithubApp, parseMagicWords, parseInstanceSettings

24 · Connect GitHub and map repositories (workspace admin)

Once the instance admin has entered the GitHub App (chapter 23), each workspace admin does two things:

  • connect a GitHub installation to the workspace, and
  • map each repository to a Plane project.

Both happen on the workspace’s GitHub Sync page.

Open the workspace page

  1. In Plane, open Workspace settings → GitHub Sync. Only workspace Admins see this entry.
  2. Or open https://<your Plane>/git-sync/ui/workspaces/<workspace-slug> directly.

The page heading is Git sync: <slug>, with four tabs:

Tab What it holds Chapter
Repositories Your personal account, the workspace GitHub connection, mapped repositories with sync health, Map a repository this chapter, 28
User links Which Plane member is which GitHub account 27
My GitHub account Your own personal link 8
Audit log What git-sync did and why 28

A member who is not an admin sees Not authorised (“Workspace settings need a workspace admin.”). Members use the direct My GitHub account link instead.

The setup checklist

While no repository is mapped, the Repositories tab shows Set up GitHub sync, a checklist of what is ready:

Line Meaning
Connect the GitHub App and choose a repository below. The next action
Rules: shipping defaults are ready; customize them after adding a mapping. Default lifecycle rules will apply (chapter 26)
Conflict policies: default policies are ready; customize them after adding a mapping. Default field policies will apply (chapter 25)
Member accounts: n linked of m. How many workspace members have linked GitHub accounts (chapter 27)
App events: verified. / need attention from an instance admin. / not yet verified; ask an instance admin to check setup. The instance’s App webhook events setup check

Connect GitHub to the workspace

Goal: one GitHub installation connected to this workspace

Before you start:

  • The instance admin has saved the App, including slug, Client ID and client secret. Otherwise the page says “Ask the instance admin to configure the GitHub App client ID, client secret and App slug.” and the buttons are disabled.
  • Connect your personal GitHub account first (My GitHub account tab → Connect personal account). git-sync uses it to prove you may connect the installation, and to list repositories you can pick.

Steps

  1. In Workspace GitHub connection, select Connect GitHub. GitHub’s App installation page opens.
  2. On GitHub, choose the account or organization, then All repositories or Only select repositories, and select Install (or Request if you are not an owner of the organization).
  3. GitHub returns you to the Setup URL. git-sync checks the installation:
    • Personal account: it must be your account.
    • Organization: you must be an active owner or admin, checked through your personal GitHub token and the App’s Members: Read permission.
  1. You land back on the page with GitHub is connected to this workspace.

Result: the installation appears as a card: the account name, “Organization · installation <id>”, Manage repository access on GitHub and Disconnect. The instance’s allow-list now holds the installation for this workspace.

The whole workspace page, with its four tabs:

Other states in the same panel:

You see Meaning Do
acme — connected Already connected to this workspace Nothing
acme — connected to another workspace One installation serves one workspace Ask that workspace’s admin, or the instance admin, to free it
acme — available + Finish connecting An installation your GitHub account can access but not yet connected Finish connecting
You see Meaning Do
acme — available + “Ask an organization owner to connect it” + Send owner handoff link You are not an owner of that organization Send a handoff link (below)
Pending organization approval — “org — requested by login. Waiting for an owner to approve.” You pressed Request on GitHub Send the owner a handoff link
“Connect your personal GitHub account to finish connecting an installation.” No personal link yet Link your account first

Press Refresh connection after anything changes on GitHub, for example after an owner approves or you add repositories to the installation.

Ask an organization owner (handoff link)

When the App must be installed or approved by an organization owner who does not use Plane:

  1. Select Send a link to an organization owner (or Send owner handoff link next to a pending request).
  2. If asked “Which GitHub organization should the owner connect? Enter its login.”, type the organization’s login, for example acme.
  3. A panel Send a link to an organization owner shows the Installation link, Copy link and when it Expires (7 days). Send the link only to the intended owner.
  4. The owner opens it, installs or approves the App on GitHub and completes GitHub authorization. They see “The account owner has connected GitHub to this workspace. You can close this page; the workspace admin can refresh the connection.” They need no Plane account.
  5. You select Refresh connection.

The link is bound to that one organization. If the owner uses it for another organization they get “This handoff link was issued for a different GitHub organization…”. It grants no Plane access.

Disconnect

Disconnect on the installation card asks “Disconnect login? Its mappings will be disabled.” After confirming, the installation is removed from this workspace’s allow-list. Every mapping that used it is Disabled until it is connected again.

Connection messages

Message Meaning
state: This connection link has expired, was already used, or belongs to another Plane account. Start again. Install links last 30 minutes, OAuth links 10 minutes, and each works once
not_yours: Your GitHub account cannot access that installation… You chose an installation your personal account cannot see
not_owner: Only an active GitHub organization owner or admin can connect its installation… Use a handoff link
taken: That installation is connected to another workspace. One workspace per installation
not_configured: Ask the instance admin to configure the GitHub App client ID, client secret and App slug. God mode incomplete
installation: GitHub did not return a valid installation… Start again and pick the intended account
Repository access updated and mappings rechecked. You changed repository selection on GitHub (Redirect on update)

Map a repository

Goal: a repository synced with one Plane project

Before you start:

  • An installation is connected.
  • Your personal GitHub account is linked and can access the repository (Triage, Write, Maintain or Admin).
  • The Plane project exists.

Steps

  1. Scroll to Map a repository.
  2. GitHub repository ① — pick from “Repositories your account can access in this workspace’s connected installations.” Use Refresh repositories after changing the installation on GitHub.
  3. Plane project ② — the project the repository’s work belongs to.
  4. Open state / Closed state — leave Project default unless you need specific states (see below).
  1. Sync direction ③ — Two-way or GitHub to Plane only. “Two-way mirrors issues both ways; GitHub to Plane only never writes back to GitHub.”
  2. Options ④:
    • Smart Commits — pre-ticked from the instance default; lets commit messages run #comment, #time and state commands.
    • Post link-back comments on GitHub — on by default; posts “Linked Plane work item: …” on PRs and issues when a link is first made.
    • Report problems as comments on GitHub and Plane — off by default; posts a short notice when a Smart Commit command or a reference fails (“Git sync could not complete this action: …”).
    • GitHub autolink references (unavailable) — disabled in this release.
  3. Select Add mapping ⑤.

Result: the panel Repository mapped appears with a Backfill offer, and the repository appears under Mapped repositories.

Open and closed states

These states apply to mirrored GitHub issues (chapter 13), not to PR automation.

Field Used when Project default means
Open state “Where an issue goes when it is reopened on GitHub (and where new open issues start).” The project’s default not-started state. New issues keep Plane’s default state.
Closed state “Where an issue goes when it is closed on GitHub.” The project’s default completed state

If you choose both, they must be different (“Choose different states for open and closed.”). Triage states are never offered.

Backfill existing work

Right after Add mapping, git-sync offers: “Link this repository’s open pull requests and issues to the Plane work items they mention.”

  • Link existing open PRs and issues now scans open PRs and issues in batches and links them by the same rules as new events. It reports “Checked n pull requests and m issues: k links made, u references did not match a work item.” If there is more, it adds “More items remain; continue to check the next batch.” with Continue.
  • Not now closes the offer. You can run it later from the mapping’s Settings tab (Run backfill).

Backfill only links open items that already mention a work item key. It does not import closed history, does not create work items and does not mirror issues that lack the plane label.

Mapped repositories

The table lists Repository, Plane project, Direction (“Two-way” / “GitHub to Plane”), a Sync health card (chapter 28), Edit and Remove.

  • Edit opens the mapping’s tabs (chapters 25–26).
  • Remove asks “Remove the mapping for owner/repo? Its rules and conflict policies are deleted too.” Links already made stay in Plane; nothing is deleted on GitHub.

Note: The browser asks first (text recorded from the running UI): “Remove the mapping for acme/website? Its rules and conflict policies are deleted too.”

If it went wrong

Symptom Cause Fix
“Connect your personal GitHub account to select a repository.” No personal link My GitHub account → Connect personal account
“Reconnect your personal GitHub account to select a repository.” Your token was rejected Reconnect
“No repositories available. Connect an installation or ask its owner to grant repository access.” No connected installation, or it does not include the repository Connect it; on GitHub add the repository to the installation; Refresh repositories
A repository you expect is missing Your own access is below Triage, or the installation does not include it Ask for access; adjust the installation
Save refused: “That GitHub installation is not allowed for this workspace” The repository’s installation is connected elsewhere or not allow-listed Connect it here or ask the instance admin
A project is missing The project is archived, or you are not a member Join the project
Mapping shows Disabled Installation disconnected or removed Reconnect, then Save changes on the mapping

What you learned

  • Workspace settings → GitHub Sync (admins only) has the tabs Repositories, User links, My GitHub account and Audit log.
  • Connect GitHub installs the App and binds that installation to this workspace. Non-owners use a 7-day, organization-bound handoff link.
  • Map a repository pairs a repository with a project: repository, project, open/closed states, Sync direction, Smart Commits, link-back and problem reports.
  • Backfill links open PRs and issues that already mention keys. Remove deletes the mapping with its rules and policies.

25 · Mapping settings and conflict policies

Every mapped repository has its own pages. Open them with Edit in Mapped repositories. The heading is the repository name (for example acme/website), with four tabs:

Tab Address Purpose
Settings /git-sync/ui/workspaces/<slug>/mappings/<id> The mapping form plus Backfill
Conflict policies …/mappings/<id>/policies Which side wins for each mirrored field
Rules …/mappings/<id>/rules What happens in Plane on each GitHub event (chapter 26)
Test rules …/mappings/<id>/dry-run Try rules without writing anything (chapter 26)

If the mapping no longer exists you see “That mapping does not exist in this workspace.” and Back to repositories.

Settings

The Settings tab shows the same fields as Map a repository (chapter 24), filled with the current values, and a Save changes button.

Field Default for a new mapping Changing it later
GitHub repository — Possible, to another repository you can access in a connected installation. Use with care: links and history stay with the old numbers.
Field Default for a new mapping Changing it later
Plane project — Possible. Custom open/closed states are reset to Project default, because states belong to a project.
Open state / Closed state Project default Affects mirrored issues from then on
Sync direction Two-way GitHub to Plane only stops every Plane-originated mirror write at once
Smart Commits Instance default (on) Takes effect for the next push
Post link-back comments on GitHub On Only new links get a comment
Report problems as comments on GitHub and Plane Off See below
GitHub autolink references (unavailable) Off, disabled Not available in this release

Below the form, Backfill offers Run backfill at any time, with Continue for further batches (chapter 24).

Saving re-verifies authority. On every save, git-sync re-checks three things:

  • that the project belongs to the workspace,
  • that the App’s installation (allow-listed for this workspace) can read the repository, and
  • for a changed repository, that your own GitHub account can access it.

If something changed meanwhile, the save fails with “The mapping changed during verification. Reload it and try again”. Saving is also how you re-enable a mapping listed as “Save the mapping to verify its installation”.

Sync direction in practice

Two-way GitHub to Plane only
GitHub issue labelled plane → creates/updates a Plane work item Yes Yes
Plane work item labelled github → creates a GitHub issue Yes No (the label is ignored)
Plane edits (title, description, state, assignees, labels, comments) → GitHub issue Yes, subject to conflict policies No, never
PR linking, Development panel, Smart Commits, lifecycle rules Yes Yes (these write to Plane)
Link-back comments and problem reports on GitHub If enabled If enabled

Choose GitHub to Plane only when GitHub is the place where issues are managed and Plane is a planning view, or for repositories outside your team’s control.

Link-back comments

When git-sync first links a PR or a mirrored issue to a work item, it posts on GitHub. Real text from the demo run:

Linked Plane work item:
- WEB-42: http://plane.example.com/acme/projects/bb57e81d-…/issues/dd4d0dfb-…

Text git-sync posted to GitHub in the demo run.

For mirrored issues the text is “Linked to Plane work item: <url>”. Each link gets one comment only, the first time. Turn the option off if your team finds the comments noisy; the Development panel in Plane works either way.

Report problems

With Report problems as comments on GitHub and Plane on, git-sync tells the author when something they wrote could not be carried out, instead of only recording it in the audit log. Examples:

  • a Smart Commit with an unknown state, a bad #time duration, or a key that matches no work item;
  • an unsigned commit when signatures are required;
  • a PR referencing a key that does not exist.

Real text from the demo run (a commit comment on GitHub):

Git sync could not complete this action:

- ` WEB-35: #shipped matches no Plane state. `
- ` WEB-35: #time needs a duration such as 1h 30m. `

Text git-sync posted to GitHub in the demo run.

The matching Plane comment on WEB-35 reads “Git sync could not complete this action: WEB-35: #shipped matches no Plane state.” Each problem is reported once. Further failures in a burst say “Additional failures are recorded in the sync audit log.”

Tip: Turn Report problems on for repositories where developers use Smart Commits. Without it, a mistyped #in-reveiw silently does nothing visible.

Conflict policies

A mirrored issue (chapter 13) exists on both sides. “Which side wins when both change the same field between syncs.” is decided per field:

Field Default Options
Title GitHub is the source of truth Last write wins, GitHub is the source of truth, Plane is the source of truth
Description GitHub is the source of truth same
State Last write wins same
Assignees Last write wins same
Field Default Options
Labels Last write wins same
Comments Last write wins same

What each policy does to a change:

Policy A change made on GitHub A change made in Plane
Last write wins Copied to Plane Copied to GitHub
GitHub is the source of truth Copied to Plane Not copied. Plane keeps its edit until the next GitHub change to that field overwrites it.
Plane is the source of truth Not copied Copied to GitHub

Last write wins does not compare clocks. Because neither Plane nor GitHub delivers events in strict order, git-sync copies the partner’s current value when it processes an event. Whichever change was made last is what both sides end up with.

Sync direction overrides policies. With GitHub to Plane only, nothing from Plane is ever applied, whatever a field’s policy says.

Goal: let Plane own the title and description

Steps

  1. Open the mapping → Conflict policies.
  2. Set Title and Description to Plane is the source of truth (or Last write wins).
  3. Select Save policies (the button shows Saving…, then Saved.).

Result: from the next edit on, title and description edits in Plane overwrite GitHub, and GitHub edits to those fields no longer reach Plane.

Note: The default makes GitHub own title and description even on a two-way mapping. Teams are often surprised that renaming a mirrored item in Plane does nothing on GitHub. That is this policy, not a fault.

Warning: Policies apply to mirrored issues only. PR links, Smart Commits and rules write to Plane regardless of policies.

What you learned

  • Each mapping has Settings, Conflict policies, Rules and Test rules tabs.
  • Settings re-verifies the project, installation and repository on every save; saving re-enables a mapping waiting for verification.
  • GitHub to Plane only stops all Plane-originated writes; link-back comments and problem reports are separate switches.
  • Conflict policies decide per field which side’s change is copied; title and description default to GitHub.

26 · Rules: lifecycle table, branch-aware rules, YAML, versions and Test rules

Rules decide what git-sync does in Plane when something happens on GitHub. A typical rule: “when a PR is merged into main, move its work items to Done”. Every mapping has one ordered list of rules. You edit it on the mapping’s Rules tab and try it safely on Test rules.

“Rules decide what happens on each GitHub event. State mappings are rules too, for example when: pull_request.merged then set_state: completed:Done.”

How rules are evaluated

Key points:

  1. First match wins. Rules are checked from the top. The first rule whose when trigger and every if condition match is used, and its actions run. No other rule runs for that event.
  2. Targets are the linked work items.
    • For PR events: every work item the PR links to (by branch, title, body, stored links or WEB-NEW).
    • For pushes: the items named in the commit messages.
  3. Tiers gate set_state only (chapter 9 explains tiers):
    • a relation link (Relates to WEB-42, or a bare key in a PR body) never changes state;
    • a non-closing link (Refs WEB-42) changes state on every trigger except pull_request.merged;
    • a closing link changes state on merge only when at least one linked PR is merged and none is still open (the merge guard; a PR that cannot be read counts as open, and the check runs only at that merge).
  4. Other actions run for every tier. That covers comments, labels, assignees, links and logged time.
  5. Finished work is never reopened by a new branch. branch.created will not move a Done or Cancelled item back.
  6. Never into Triage. A state target in the triage group is refused.

The shipping defaults

If you never save rules, this table applies (chapter 14 shows it from a developer’s view):

Lifecycle point Trigger Default target
Branch pushed branch.created started:In Progress
PR drafted pull_request.drafted started:In Progress
PR opened pull_request.opened (also ready for review) started:In Progress
Review requested pull_request.review_requested started:In Review
Changes requested pull_request.changes_requested no change
PR approved pull_request.approved no change
Ready for merge pull_request.ready_for_merge no change
Lifecycle point Trigger Default target
PR merged pull_request.merged, base branch matching ^main$ completed:Done
PR closed without merge pull_request.closed_unmerged no change
PR reopened pull_request.reopened no change

State targets

A target can be written three ways:

Form Example Resolves to
group:Name started:In Review The state named In Review in the started group. If no such name exists but the group has exactly one state, that one. Otherwise the rule fails and is audited “state … does not exist”.
group completed The group’s default state, otherwise the group’s first state
Name In QA The state with that name, only if exactly one state in the project has it (case-insensitive)

Groups are backlog, unstarted, started, completed, cancelled (and triage, which automation refuses).

Warning: A project that has several started states but none called In Review makes the review-requested default fail. Either create In Review or change that row of the table.

Rules tab — lifecycle mapping table

Open the mapping → Rules. The status line says either “Using shipping defaults (not saved yet).” or “Saved version n.” Two editing modes are offered: Lifecycle mapping table and Raw YAML editor.

Goal: change what a lifecycle point does

Steps

  1. Under Lifecycle points → Plane state (“Choose a project state for each event. Leave it empty for no state change.”), pick a Target state for any Lifecycle event:
    • Branch pushed, PR drafted, PR opened, Review requested, Changes requested, PR approved, Ready for merge, PR merged, PR closed without merge, PR reopened.
    • The picker offers each project state (“In Review · In progress”), each group (“Completed (any matching state)”) and No state change.
  2. Optionally change Merged base-branch regex (“The PR base branch must match this regex for the merged state to apply (default: ^main$).”). For example ^(main|master)$.
  3. Select Save mapping table.

Result: a new rule version is saved and used from the next event.

Note: Ready for merge fires once per head commit when the PR is open and not a draft, has at least one standing approval and no standing “changes requested”, and all checks and the combined commit status are successful (neutral and skipped count as success). Map it to a state such as Ready to merge if your team wants the board to show it.

Branch-aware rules

“Evaluated before defaults; first match wins. Useful for staging/release branch flows.”

Goal: merging into staging moves work to In QA, merging into main to Done

Steps

  1. Select + Add branch rule.
  2. Base branch (regex): ^staging$. ①
  3. Lifecycle: PR merged. ② (For Branch pushed the base column shows “N/A (branch has no base)”.)
  4. Target state: In QA (or started:In QA). ③
  5. Keep the table’s PR merged row at Done with Merged base-branch regex ^main$.
  6. Save mapping table.

Result: the compiled YAML puts the branch rule first:

- name: merged into ^staging$
  when: pull_request.merged
  if:
    base_branch: ^staging$
  then:
    - set_state: started:In QA
- name: "default: branch_pushed"
  when: branch.created
  then:
    - set_state: started:In Progress
# … the other defaults …
- name: "default: merged"
  when: pull_request.merged
  if:
    base_branch: ^main$
  then:
    - set_state: completed:Done

In the demo run, PR #126 merged into staging moved WEB-39 to In QA; PR #121 merged into main moved WEB-42 to Done.

Rules tab — raw YAML editor

Choose Raw YAML editor for anything the table cannot express: labels, comments, links, assignees, logged time, issue/check/deployment triggers.

Goal: write and save a custom rule

Steps

  1. In Rules (YAML) (“Use lifecycle, branch, push, check, deployment, issue or comment triggers. Test rules before saving.”), edit the list.
  2. Test it on Test rules first (below).
  3. Select Validate and save YAML. Invalid rules are refused with a message naming the rule, for example Rule at index 2: unknown trigger pull_request.merge.

To change only the state of one rule without retyping YAML, choose Rule to update (“Rule n · triggers”), pick a Target state, and select Apply state to selected rule.

Warning: Switching between modes can replace work.

  • Leaving YAML for the table with custom rules asks: “The current YAML contains custom rules or manual edits that cannot be represented in the table. Switching to table mode will replace your rules with defaults upon save. Discard custom YAML?”
  • Saving the table over custom YAML asks: “Saving the mapping table will overwrite your custom YAML rules. Overwrite?”

Rule format

- name: Optional label shown in the audit log      # optional
  when: pull_request.merged                       # one trigger or a list
  if:                                             # optional; all must match
    base_branch: "^release/"
  then:                                           # one or more actions, one key each
    - set_state: "completed:Done"
    - comment: "Released in {{release}}"

Triggers (when)

Trigger Fires on
pull_request.drafted, .opened, .review_requested, .changes_requested, .approved, .ready_for_merge, .merged, .closed_unmerged, .reopened PR lifecycle points
pull_request.* Any of the above
branch.created First push of a new branch
push Any push (items named in commit messages)
commit.pushed_to_default A push to the default branch
check_suite.<conclusion> e.g. check_suite.success, check_suite.failure; check_suite.* CI results
deployment_status.<state> e.g. deployment_status.success; deployment_status.* Deployments
issue.<action> e.g. issue.opened, issue.closed; issue.* Issue events (GitHub or Plane)
comment.<action> e.g. comment.created; comment.* Issue comments

Conditions (if)

Key Value Matching
base_branch regex PR base branch
head_branch regex PR head branch, pushed branch, deployment ref
labels_any list At least one label present (exact case)
labels_all list All labels present (exact case)
author login or list GitHub login of the event sender, case-insensitive
repo owner/name or list Case-insensitive
Key Value Matching
project Plane project UUID or list Exact

Actions (then)

Action Value Effect in Plane Gated by tier?
set_state state target Move the item Yes
add_label label name Add a label (created if missing) No
remove_label label name Remove a label No
assign GitHub login Add the linked Plane member as assignee (skipped if unlinked) No
comment text Comment on the item No
add_link {url, title} Add a link to the item No
log_time duration Comment “Time logged: duration” (Plane CE has no worklog) No
create_issue {project, title} Create a work item in that project (identifier or UUID); once per event No

Text values may use {{path}} templates filled from the event context, for example {{issue.title}} or {{comment.url}}. A template that cannot be resolved fails the rule, which is audited.

Example: label and announce failing builds

- name: Failing CI
  when: check_suite.failure
  then:
    - add_label: ci-failing
    - comment: "CI failed on the linked pull request."
- name: CI fixed
  when: check_suite.success
  then:
    - remove_label: ci-failing

Rule versions

Every save (table or YAML) creates a new version. Rule versions lists Version, Saved by, Saved at and Action; the newest is “n (current)”.

Restore asks “Restore version n? This creates a new version and replaces unsaved editor changes.” Restoring never deletes history; it saves the old rules as a new current version.

Test rules (dry run)

“Run a delivery through the rules without writing anything. Leave the rules empty to use this mapping’s saved rules.”

Goal: prove a rule does what you expect before saving it

Steps

  1. Test input: choose one of two modes.
    • Webhook delivery: choose Source (GitHub or Plane) and Event. Then either paste a Payload (JSON), or enter Recorded delivery (audit entry id) (“Uses the payload stored in the audit log instead of the one below.”). Audit entry ids are on the Audit log.
    • Specific rule trigger: type a Rule trigger (suggestions offered) and a Rule context (JSON) (“Optional fields: repo, project, author, base_branch, head_branch, labels, context (for templates). Use {} to test only the trigger.”).
  2. Optionally paste Rules to test (YAML, optional). If empty, the saved rules (or the defaults) are used.
  3. Select Run dry-run.

Example input (specific rule trigger):

Rule trigger:  pull_request.merged
Rule context:  {"base_branch": "staging", "repo": "acme/website"}

Result:

  • A match shows “Trigger: pull_request.merged. Matched rule 1 (merged into ^staging$).” followed by the actions as JSON.
  • No match shows “Trigger: … No rule matched.” and No actions would run.
  • A delivery that is not an automation event shows “That delivery is not an automation event.”

To try rules before saving them, paste them into Rules to test (YAML, optional). The dry-run then uses those rules instead of the saved ones and still writes nothing:

A dry run shows rule selection and the actions. It does not check that a state exists in the project or that the write would be allowed for a given tier. Those are checked when the rule really runs, and failures appear in the audit log as Automation rule matched with outcome failed or ignored.

If it went wrong

Symptom Likely cause Check
A PR merge did not move the item to Done Base branch does not match ^main$; link is non-closing/relation; another linked PR still open; no matching rule Audit log: Automation rule matched outcome ignored, or no entry; Test rules with the base branch
“Automation rule matched … failed: state … does not exist” Target state name not in this project Fix the target or create the state
A branch rule never fires It sits after a broader rule that matches first Move it up; branch rules from the table are always first
Labels condition never matches Case differs Labels compare exactly
Custom YAML disappeared Saved the table over it Rule versions → Restore

What you learned

  • Rules are an ordered list; the first matching rule wins and its actions run on the linked items.
  • Tiers gate only set_state; the merge guard protects multi-PR work.
  • The lifecycle table and branch-aware rules compile to YAML; the YAML editor exposes every trigger, condition and action.
  • Every save is a version you can restore; Test rules shows matches and actions without writing anything.

Source files

  • src/rules/engine.ts, src/rules/types.ts — grammar and evaluation
  • src/github/pr-automation.ts — QLL_DEFAULTS, compileLifecycleRules, state resolution, tier gating, ready for merge
  • src/app/rules.ts, src/app/rule-events.ts — live execution and event translation
  • src/ui/client/Workspace.tsx, rule-editor.ts — Rules and Test rules tabs
  • src/ui/dry-run.ts — dry-run endpoint

27 · User links

A user link pairs a Plane member with a GitHub account in one workspace. git-sync uses user links to:

  • recognize who did something on GitHub. The webhook’s authenticated sender (never the commit author name) is translated to a Plane member for Smart Commit provenance (“via sha by login”), assignee and @mention translation, and rule assign actions;
  • write Plane → GitHub mirror changes as that person when their personal token works, instead of as the App;
  • fill the Branch name {username} placeholder and the repository picker for that member.

Note: In this release every write into Plane is made by the service account (the bot), even when the GitHub user is linked. A link improves attribution in GitHub and in git-sync’s records; it does not make Plane show the member as the author.

There are three ways a link is made:

How Who Stores a personal token? Chapter
The member uses Connect personal account (GitHub OAuth) The member Yes, encrypted 8
An admin uses Link a user on this page Workspace admin No this chapter
Automatic email match: an unlinked GitHub sender whose public GitHub email equals exactly one member’s Plane email git-sync No this chapter

Open the page

Workspace settings → GitHub Sync → User links, or /git-sync/ui/workspaces/<slug>/users.

Linked GitHub accounts lists Plane member and GitHub account for every link. In the demo:

  • Jordan Admin (jordan-acme) and Alex Developer (alex-dev) connected themselves;
  • Sam Reviewer (sam-reviews) was linked by the admin.

A row marked “Needs re-authorization. Reconnect using this member’s own Plane session.” means GitHub refused that member’s stored token, for example because they revoked the App on GitHub. Until they Reconnect on My GitHub account, their mirror writes fall back to the App. Admins cannot reconnect for them.

With no links, the page says “No Plane users are linked to GitHub accounts yet. Unlinked users are attributed to the service account.”

Link a user manually

Goal: tell git-sync that a Plane member is a given GitHub account

Before you start: the person must be a member of this workspace. Ask them for their GitHub username.

Steps

  1. Under Link a user, choose Plane member. ①
  2. Type GitHub username. ②
  3. Select Look up id. ③ git-sync asks GitHub for the account and fills GitHub user id (“Numeric and stable across renames.”). If GitHub does not know the login you see Lookup failed.
  4. Select Link account. ④

After Link account the new link appears in the list at once:

Result: the link appears in the list with GitHub’s canonical spelling of the login.

Checks git-sync makes on save:

Refusal Why
“That GitHub account does not exist” The login is unknown on your GitHub host
“githubId does not match that GitHub login” The id you typed is not that account’s id; use Look up id
Refusal Why
“That Plane user is not a member of this workspace” Only members can be linked
“githubLogin is not a valid GitHub username” Typo
A uniqueness error That GitHub account is already linked to another member; one GitHub account can be linked to only one member per workspace

Links are keyed by GitHub’s numeric id, so a later rename on GitHub does not break them.

Unlink

Unlink asks “Unlink login? Any credentials stored for this user are deleted.” After confirming:

  • the link is removed and the member’s stored GitHub token (if any) is deleted;
  • git-sync remembers the unlink, so automatic email matching will not re-link that GitHub account. Only an explicit Link account or the member’s own Connect personal account links it again;
  • future events from that GitHub account are attributed to the service identity and audited as Service account attribution.

Note: The browser asks first (text recorded from the running UI): “Unlink alex-dev? Any credentials stored for this user are deleted.”

Automatic email matching

When an event arrives from a GitHub sender with no link, git-sync tries one careful match:

  1. It reads the sender’s public GitHub profile email.
  2. It compares it with the email addresses of the workspace’s Plane members.
  3. If exactly one member matches, it links them and audits Account matched by email.
  4. If there is no public email, no match or several matches, it links nobody and audits the reason.

Bots (*[bot], ghost, accounts of type Bot) are never matched, nothing is guessed, and an unlinked account is never matched again automatically.

Member accounts in the setup checklist

While a workspace has no mappings, Set up GitHub sync shows “Member accounts: n linked of m.” It links to this page. Aim for every developer who pushes code to be linked before you rely on Smart Commits.

If it went wrong

Symptom Cause Fix
Smart Commit comments say “by login” but the audit shows Service account attribution That GitHub login is not linked in this workspace Link it
A member’s mirror edits on GitHub appear as the App No personal token, or token needs re-authorization Member uses Connect personal account / Reconnect
Assignee from GitHub not copied to Plane The GitHub assignee is not linked Link the user; unlinked assignees are dropped
An unlinked person keeps getting re-linked It does not happen: unlinks are remembered —

What you learned

  • User links map Plane members to stable GitHub ids for attribution, assignees, mentions and the repository picker.
  • Members connect themselves via OAuth; admins can link by username with Look up id; careful public-email matching links only exact single matches.
  • Unlink deletes stored credentials and stops email re-matching.
  • Plane-side writes still come from the bot in this release.
